species.name: Australian salmon
species.conditions: Local closures still apply.
species.identify: Streamlined fish; forked tail; small dark spots on upper sides.
species.bait: Pilchard pieces; small baitfish; metal slices.
species.where: Surf gutters, estuary mouths and visible bait schools.
species.when: Try dawn or dusk with moving water; watch feeding birds.
species.rig: Cast beyond the gutter edge. Retrieve a metal steadily or fish a single bait hook.

species.name: Bream (black / yellowfin)
species.conditions: Combined with tarwhine.
species.identify: Deep body and spiny dorsal. Illustration shows yellowfin bream; black bream has darker fins.
species.bait: Peeled prawn, marine worms, nippers or small fish strips.
species.where: Estuary structure: oyster edges, pylons and rocky banks.
species.when: Try a rising tide or low light; fish close to cover.
species.rig: Light running sinker; small non-offset circle hook. Use just enough weight to reach the bait zone.

species.name: Dusky flathead
species.conditions: Release fish outside the size range.
species.identify: Broad flat head; eyes on top; tapering body; dark mark on lower tail. Check against other flatheads.
species.bait: Fresh prawn, whitebait or legally collected poddy mullet.
species.where: Sand flats, channel drop-offs and creek mouths.
species.when: Often productive October-April; work a moving tide.
species.rig: Running sinker and 1/0-4/0 non-offset circle hook. Or hop a soft plastic along the bottom.

species.name: Eastern blue groper
species.conditions: No taking. Includes blue, brown and red forms.
species.identify: Thick lips; deep wrasse body; rounded tail. Adults may be blue; females and juveniles brown/red.
species.bait: Protected species: do not target.
species.where: Rocky reefs and kelp habitat.
species.when: Observe rather than fish for this species.
species.rig: If caught accidentally, handle gently and release promptly. Colour alone does not identify a groper.

species.name: Luderick
species.conditions: Local closures still apply.
species.identify: Deep body with dark vertical bars; small mouth; forked tail.
species.bait: Green weed or cabbage weed; artificial weed flies.
species.where: Weedy estuary walls, bridge pylons and rocky edges.
species.when: Year-round; try a moving tide with a controlled drift.
species.rig: Use a stem float (an upright bite indicator), split shot (small pinch-on weights) and a size 6 or 8 sneck hook. Size 8 is smaller than size 6. Adjust the float-to-hook distance so weed bait hangs near the fish’s feeding depth. Take up loose line and lift the rod gently when a bite pulls the float under.

rig_links.heading: Choose the depth and watch for a bite

species.name: Mulloway
species.conditions: Boat/day: 2 with 2+ fishers; charter: 3.
species.identify: Long robust body; rounded tail; bright lateral line; dark spot above pectoral base.
species.bait: Fresh squid, fish strips or legally collected live bait.
species.where: Deep estuary holes, channel edges and surf gutters.
species.when: Try low light around a tide change; allow time for a bite.
species.rig: Running sinker and strong leader. Match hook to bait; let a circle hook load before winding.

species.name: Sand whiting
species.conditions: Combined across whiting species.
species.identify: Slender body; pointed snout; small mouth; two dorsal fins. Similar whiting need closer checks.
species.bait: Marine worms, nippers or peeled prawn.
species.where: Shallow sandy flats, channel edges and surf gutters.
species.when: Rising tide on flats; warmer months for surface lures.
species.rig: Light running sinker and small long-shank hook. Keep worm bait neat and close to the bottom.

species.name: Silver trevally
species.conditions: Combined across trevallies.
species.identify: Deep silver body; long curved pectoral fin; forked tail; dark gill-cover mark.
species.bait: Small prawn pieces, pilchard pieces or soft plastics.
species.where: Estuary channels, deeper edges and sheltered reef.
species.when: Try dawn or dusk with tidal flow.
species.rig: Light running sinker; drift small baits naturally. Lift steadily rather than jerking soft mouths.

species.name: Snapper
species.conditions: Local closures still apply.
species.identify: Deep body; spiny dorsal; small spots on upper sides. Large adults may develop a forehead bump.
species.bait: Squid strips, pilchard pieces or soft plastics.
species.where: Reef edges, broken rocky bottom and adjacent sand.
species.when: Try dawn or dusk; choose manageable current and swell.
species.rig: Single-hook paternoster for depth, or lightly weighted bait over reef edges. Keep bait near the bottom.

species.name: Tailor
species.conditions: Local closures still apply.
species.identify: Strong toothed jaws; streamlined body; two dorsal fins and forked tail.
species.bait: Pilchard or fish strips; metal lures.
species.where: Surf gutters, estuary entrances and bait schools.
species.when: Try dawn/dusk when baitfish are active.
species.rig: Cast a metal lure and retrieve steadily. For bait, use an abrasion-resistant leader and keep tension.

species.name: Tarwhine
species.conditions: Combined with black and yellowfin bream.
species.identify: Rounded forehead; deep body; horizontal scale lines. Often confused with bream.
species.bait: Marine worms, peeled prawn or small shellfish baits.
species.where: Sandy areas beside rocky reef, surf gutters and estuaries.
species.when: Try moving tides; low light can help in shallow water.
species.rig: Light running sinker with a small bait hook. Keep the bait near sand and reef edges.

species.name: Yellowtail kingfish
species.conditions: Local closures still apply.
species.identify: Long torpedo shape; deeply forked tail; long second dorsal and anal fins. Colour stripe is not visible here.
species.bait: Fresh squid, legally collected live bait or jigs.
species.where: Reef structure, channel markers and bait schools.
species.when: Try moving water and early light; follow bait activity.
species.rig: Strong tackle and leader around structure. Present squid naturally; use a suitably sized single hook.

species.name: Golden perch
species.conditions: All year; local closures still apply.
species.identify: Deep stout body; large mouth; arched back and rounded tail.
species.bait: Freshwater shrimp, small yabbies, worms or diving lures.
species.where: Murray-Darling rivers and stocked dams; snags and rocky points.
species.when: Try warmer water and late afternoon; work structure slowly.
species.rig: Light running sinker beside cover or slow lure retrieve. Match hook to bait and keep its point clear.

species.name: Longfin eel
species.conditions: All year; possession is not double the daily bag.
species.identify: Mottled eel; dorsal fin begins clearly before the anal fin. Compare fin origins with shortfin eel.
species.bait: Earthworms or fish pieces.
species.where: Freshwater rivers, dams and lakes east of the Divide.
species.when: Try dusk and after dark in calm sheltered water.
species.rig: Running sinker to present bait near the bottom. Use a secure leader; wet hands before handling.

species.name: Murray cod
species.conditions: Closed Sep-Nov except Copeton and Blowering dams.
species.identify: Broad head and large mouth; mottled body; rounded tail. Do not confuse with protected trout cod.
species.bait: Yabbies, bardi grubs or large diving/surface lures.
species.where: Murray-Darling waterways; submerged timber and rocky cover.
species.when: Open season: Dec-Aug; Copeton/Blowering exceptions. Try low light.
species.rig: Strong leader near snags. Work a lure slowly past cover; support the fish horizontally for release.

species.name: Southern shortfin eel
species.conditions: All year; possession is not double the daily bag.
species.identify: Plain eel; dorsal origin approximately level with anal origin. Check fins, not body colour alone.
species.bait: Earthworms or fish pieces.
species.where: Coastal freshwater rivers, lakes and dams east of the Divide.
species.when: Try dusk/after dark beside sheltered bottom structure.
species.rig: Running sinker and single bait hook. Keep weight light enough for natural bait presentation.

species.name: Eel-tailed catfish
species.conditions: Eastern waters and listed western dams only. No take in western rivers or unlisted western dams.
species.identify: Broad head with barbels; scaleless body; eel-like tail. Dorsal and anal fins join around tail; sharp fin spines.
species.bait: Earthworms or small yabbies. Bottom-feeding fish: place bait near the bed.
species.where: Eastern rivers/dams or listed western dams: sheltered pools and soft-bottom margins.
species.when: Try dusk/after dark; a starting point, not a guaranteed bite time.
species.rig: Light running sinker, swivel, leader and single bait hook. Keep point clear; take care around fin spines.

species.name: European carp
species.conditions: Do not move live carp between waters or use live finfish as inland bait.
species.identify: Large scales; long dorsal fin; fleshy downturned mouth with two pairs of barbels. Not bony bream.
species.bait: Corn, bread or earthworms. Present a small bait on or near the bottom.
species.where: Slow rivers, sheltered lake margins and soft-bottom shallows.
species.when: Try warmer water and quiet early/late periods; watch feeding activity.
species.rig: Light running sinker or float. Keep bait small and point clear; carp take baits from the bed.

species.name: Bony bream
species.conditions: Combined with other native finfish without a separate limit. Do not use live finfish as inland bait.
species.identify: Deep silver herring-shaped body; blunt snout; long last dorsal ray; sharp ridge of belly scales. No barbels.
species.bait: Mainly algae and detritus feeders; usually not a bait-and-hook target.
species.where: Lowland inland rivers, lakes and backwaters, often in schools.
species.when: Look for schooling activity in calmer water; useful to recognise among other catches.
species.rig: Identify and observe. Do not use live bony bream as inland bait or move fish between waterways.

species.name: Barramundi
species.conditions: Northern Australia / stocked-venue reference. Size, bag and seasonal rules vary by state and venue; NSW limits cannot be assumed.
species.identify: Large upturned mouth with projecting lower jaw; large scales; notched dorsal and rounded tail.
species.bait: Prawn/fish-style soft plastics or diving lures; permitted bait varies by region.
species.where: Northern Australian fresh/tidal waters and stocked dams. NSW: authorised stocked venues only.
species.when: Try warm water and low light around cover; check local closed seasons first.
species.rig: Abrasion-resistant leader beside timber. Work a lure slowly past cover; support heavy fish horizontally.

species.name: Australian bass
species.conditions: Combined bass/estuary perch. Rivers: only 1 over 35 cm. Below dams: no take May-Aug, catch/release permitted. All year in dams and rivers above dams.
species.identify: Oval compressed body; dark back; large mouth; notched dorsal; slightly forked tail. Compare estuary perch.
species.bait: Earthworms, crickets, small diving lures, spinnerbaits or surface lures.
species.where: Eastern rivers and stocked dams; shaded banks, snags and weed edges.
species.when: Try dawn/dusk for surface lures, deeper cover in daylight. Seasonal take restrictions apply.
species.rig: Cast beside cover and retrieve slowly. Light tackle with a leader suited to snags; avoid dragging fish through weed.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.conditions: Combined trout/salmon. Streams close after June long weekend until October long weekend. Spawning 1/2 limits apply May to June long weekend; Oct-Apr use fly/lure limits. Dams open all year. Check water class and local exceptions.
species.identify: Streamlined body; small adipose fin; black spots on tail and back. Pink side band cannot be shown in monochrome.
species.bait: Worms, insects, small spinners or flies, where that water class permits bait.
species.where: Cool upland streams and stocked lakes such as the Snowy Mountains and New England.
species.when: Try cool morning/evening water. Follow stream seasons; fish deeper when lakes warm.
species.rig: Small lure or fly on a light leader. Present upstream in streams; bait rigs only where permitted.

species.name: Brown trout
species.conditions: Combined trout/salmon. Streams close after June long weekend until October long weekend. Spawning 1/2 limits apply May to June long weekend; Oct-Apr use fly/lure limits. Dams open all year. Check water class and local exceptions.
species.identify: Small adipose fin; larger scattered flank spots, often haloed; tail mostly plain and squarer than rainbow trout.
species.bait: Small minnow lures, insect flies or worms where bait is permitted.
species.where: Cool streams, shaded undercuts and stocked upland lakes.
species.when: Try low light and insect hatches; follow water-specific stream seasons.
species.rig: Approach quietly and cast beyond cover. Drift flies naturally or retrieve a small lure near banks.

species.name: Silver perch
species.conditions: Listed stocked dams only. No take from rivers, tributaries or unlisted dams.
species.identify: Deep oval body with small head and mouth; large regular scales; forked tail. Not yellowfin/black bream.
species.bait: Worms, freshwater shrimp or small yabbies in permitted listed dams.
species.where: Listed stocked dams; sheltered margins, flooded grass and sloping banks.
species.when: Try warmer months and early/late periods; move if small fish repeatedly steal bait.
species.rig: Small bait and light running sinker or float. Keep point exposed; handle gently for release.

species.name: Redfin perch
species.conditions: NSW pest: do not return to water. Illegal to possess live redfin or use live/dead redfin as bait.
species.identify: Dark vertical bars; two separate dorsal fins; dark patch at rear of first dorsal. Red fins are not visible here.
species.bait: Worms, small spinners, soft plastics or ice jigs. Do not use redfin as bait.
species.where: Cooler lakes and slow rivers; schools near weed, timber and drop-offs.
species.when: Try daylight beside structure; a caught fish may indicate a nearby school.
species.rig: Light spinning tackle; slow hops close to bottom. NSW advice is to keep redfin out of the water, not release them.

species.name: Estuary perch
species.conditions: Combined bass/estuary perch. Rivers: only 1 over 35 cm. Below dams: no take May-Aug, catch/release permitted. All year in dams and rivers above dams.
species.identify: Large upturned mouth and concave forehead; deep compressed body; notched dorsal. Compare Australian bass.
species.bait: Small prawn-style plastics, diving lures, worms or shrimp where permitted.
species.where: Brackish estuaries and lower freshwater reaches; pylons, timber and deeper edges.
species.when: Try low light with moving water in tidal reaches; observe seasonal take restrictions.
species.rig: Cast beside structure, allow the lure to sink and retrieve slowly. Keep leader clear of abrasion.

species.name: Freshwater yabby
species.conditions: NSW freshwater yabby rules. All year, subject to local closures. Yabby traps prohibited in inland waters; check permitted hoop/open-pyramid nets and water-specific restrictions. Do not confuse with saltwater nippers or spiny crayfish.
species.identify: Smooth-shelled freshwater crayfish with two large front claws and a segmented tail. Do not identify by colour alone; distinguish spiny crayfish.
species.bait: Check local permitted bait and collection methods before setting gear.
species.where: Still or slow muddy freshwater, dams, lakes and billabongs.
species.when: Open all year under the NSW species table; check local closures and water access.
species.rig: Use only permitted collection gear. Check dimensions, marking, quantities and trout-water restrictions on the official methods page.

topics.title: Hooks & setting the hook
topics.left: Point turns toward the shank. Use non-offset circles for bait; leave the gape clear. Let the rod load and wind steadily instead of striking.
topics.right: The more open point suits worm baits. A long shank helps thread bait. Keep contact and lift smoothly to set it; match hook size to the bait.
topics.caption: Circle points turn inward; J hooks point up. Match the hook gape to your bait.

note_sections.title: Name the parts
note_sections.text: The eye is where you tie the line. The shank is the straight section below it; the bend curves around towards the sharp point. The gape is the gap between point and shank. Keep the point and that gap clear enough to catch in the fish’s mouth.

note_sections.title: Compare hook types
note_sections.text: Photographs show real tackle; separate monochrome schematics keep the shape visible at LilyGO size. Examples are not to scale. | Type | Real example | LilyGO · 140×76 | What to notice | How to use it | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Sneck** | | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/sneck-hook-lilygo.png\|140]] | A squarer bend and an exposed point; the pictured Mustad model has a long straight shank. | Small weed-bait hooks suit luderick; take up loose line and lift smoothly on a bite. | | **J hook / long shank** | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/j-hook-photo.png\|140]] | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/j-hook-lilygo.png\|140]] | The bend resembles a J; long-shank versions extend the straight section. | Choose a shank that holds the bait neatly; leave the point clear and set with a smooth lift. | | **Circle hook** | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/circle-hook-photo.png\|140]] | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/circle-hook-lilygo.png\|140]] | The point curves inward towards the shank. | Let the line tighten and wind steadily; do not make a sharp strike. |

note_sections.title: What is a sneck hook?
note_sections.text:
Sneck names a traditional hook pattern: it describes the shape, not the size or a special knot. Small sneck hooks are commonly used with weed bait for luderick. They are ordinary single-point hooks, rather than circle hooks.

“Size 6–8 sneck hook” means a sneck-pattern hook in that size range, such as size 6 or size 8. It does not mean 6–8 centimetres. Put a small amount of weed on the hook, leaving the point exposed.

note_sections.title: How hook sizes work
note_sections.text:
For common numbered sizes, a larger number means a smaller hook: **size 10 → 8 → 6 → 4 → 2 → 1**, from smaller to larger. So size 8 is smaller than size 6 within the same pattern.

After size 1, the scale changes to **1/0 → 2/0 → 3/0**, increasing in size. These are called “one aught”, “two aught” and so on. Size 6 and size 6/0 are very different; 6/0 is much larger.

Numbers are size labels, not lengths in millimetres. Actual dimensions vary between hook patterns and manufacturers. Compare the hook itself, including the gape and wire thickness, and match it to the bait and fish’s mouth.

note_sections.title: Setting a sneck or J hook
note_sections.text:
Setting the hook means making its point take hold in the fish’s mouth. With a luderick float rig and sneck hook, take up slack and lift the rod smoothly when a bite pulls the float under. Avoid a hard yank that can tear the hook out.

A long-shank hook has an extended straight section that can help hold a long bait such as a worm.

note_sections.title: Circle hooks work differently
note_sections.text: A circle hook has a point that curves inward towards the shank. When a fish takes the bait, let the line tighten and wind steadily so the hook can turn into the corner of the mouth. Do not use the sharp lifting strike associated with a J hook. Keep the point and gape clear of bait.

topics.title: Floats / bobbers
topics.left: Sensitive bite indicators for small baits. Add split shot so only the tip shows; set bait depth beside weed or structure.
topics.right: A buoyant float for larger baits. A sliding float uses a stop to control depth. Float size must support the bait and weights without being pulled under.
topics.caption: A float keeps bait at a chosen depth and shows bites. Weight it so the tip remains visible.

note_sections.title: What is a float?
note_sections.text: A float, also called a bobber, is a buoyant bite indicator attached to fishing line. It supports the bait at a chosen depth and moves when something pulls the line. The visible tip is the part you watch.

note_sections.title: Compare float types
note_sections.text:
Photographs show real tackle; separate monochrome schematics keep the shape visible at LilyGO size. Examples are not to scale.

| Type | Real example | LilyGO · 140×76 | What to notice | How to use it |

This photo shows a foam bobber, not a cork-bodied model. | Match buoyancy to bait and weights. Bobby corks serve a similar role; attachment varies by model. |

note_sections.title: Stem floats and wagglers
note_sections.text:
A stem float has a slender stem and a buoyant body. Small weights below it help it stand upright. This makes gentle pulls easier to see. Stem or pencil-style floats are commonly used for luderick.

A waggler is a float attached to the line at its bottom end. Attachment methods vary: use the sleeves, eye or adaptor intended for your float rather than assuming every float clips on the same way.

note_sections.title: Fixed versus sliding floats
note_sections.text:
A fixed float stays at the position you choose on the line. Moving it farther from the hook increases the bait depth.

A sliding float lets line run through it until a float stop reaches it. The stop is a small knot or stopper set on the line to limit travel. This helps when fishing deeper than a fixed float is comfortable to cast. A bobby cork is a buoyant float often used with larger baits.

note_sections.title: Balance it in the water
note_sections.text: Add small weights until the body is mostly underwater and the tip remains visible. The bait and weights must not pull the float under by themselves. A float lying flat may need more weight; one sinking continuously may have too much. Test with the bait attached.

note_sections.title: Still water, rivers and tidal estuaries
note_sections.text:
Floats are not just for lakes. Use them wherever keeping bait at a chosen depth and watching a bite indicator suits the fish and conditions.

In still water, present bait beside feeding areas such as weed beds, reeds, submerged timber or a drop-off. In moving water, let it drift along a current edge or past cover, and adjust depth so it does not continually drag on the bottom. Wind and waves can also move a float on a lake.

**Structure** means physical features fish use for food or shelter: rocks, weeds, fallen trees, bridge pylons and changes in depth. Fish behaviour matters as much as the place. Luderick feed around weed-covered rocks and walls; a natural weed-bait drift can bring the bait to them. Other species may feed near the bottom, hunt beside cover or move through open water.

Choose float buoyancy for bait, weights, current and visibility. A delicate float can show gentle bites in calm water; stronger current or rough water may require a more buoyant model. A bigger float is not automatically better.

See [[Hobbies/Fishing/Rigs/Swivels, snaps & leaders#Why line gets curly or tangled|line memory, twist and loose loops]] if the line coils or tangles during a drift.

note_sections.title: Where fish sit around structure
note_sections.text:
## Still water: edges, shade and cover

![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/fish-structure-still-water.svg|600]]

Look beside weed edges, fallen timber and the boundary between shallow and deeper water. Cover offers shelter and food; a nearby depth change gives fish access to another depth. Present bait beside the cover rather than casting straight into branches or thick weed.

## Moving water: current breaks and feeding lanes

![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/fish-structure-moving-water.svg|600]]

A rock, pylon or bank feature can slow the water behind it. Fish may hold in that slower pocket, often facing into the flow, and feed near the **current seam**: the boundary between faster and slower water. Let a float drift along that boundary with the bait at feeding depth.

The diagrams show common places to look, not a rule for every species. Luderick also graze weed-covered rocks and walls; their feeding depth may differ from the fish shown. In tidal water, observe the actual flow: the sheltered side can change when the current reverses.

topics.title: Sinker types
topics.left: A through-hole lets these weights slide on line. Use in a running rig. Split shot clamps onto line to trim float balance.
topics.right: An end attachment suits a paternoster. Use the lightest weight that reaches and holds the feeding zone; increase it when current carries bait away.
topics.caption: Sliding weights, clip-on shot and end weights do different jobs. Use only the weight you need.

note_sections.title: What is a sinker?
note_sections.text: A sinker is a weight attached to fishing line. It helps bait sink, holds it against current, or balances a float. Use only enough weight to do the job.

note_sections.text:
Photographs show real tackle; the monochrome drawings keep the main shape and attachment visible at LilyGO size. Examples are not to scale. Bomb and drop names overlap between manufacturers.

note_sections.title: Split shot: small pinch-on weights
note_sections.text:
Split shot are tiny round or oval weights with a slit. Put the line into the slit and close it gently with the appropriate tool. Do not use your teeth. Excessive squeezing can damage the line.

For a float rig, place shot below the float and above the hook. Add or remove a little at a time until the float stands upright with its tip visible. The weights help the bait sink; they do not sit on the hook.

note_sections.title: Photo credits
note_sections.text: Split shot: [Mx. Granger](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Split_shot_3.jpg). Other examples: [Ruff tuff cream puff](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fishing_weights_smaller_sizes.jpg). Both photographs are [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/); selected views are shown. The split shot photo is a removable model with extra tabs. The LilyGO drawings are separate schematics.

note_sections.title: Where to put split shot
note_sections.text:
Split shot is pinched onto the fishing line, not tied on. Put the line into the slit and close it gently so the weight stays in place. Some removable models have tabs for opening them again. If a shot slides freely, it is not gripping properly; reposition or replace it rather than crushing the line.

Place it **below the float and above the hook**. For a luderick rig, keep the lowest shot about **20 cm or more above the hook** as a starting arrangement, then adjust for the bait, float and current. This is not a fixed distance for every rig.

![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/split-shot-placement.svg|600]]

note_sections.title: Bait distance, slack and bite contact
note_sections.text:
The bait goes **on the hook** in this weed-bait rig. There is no separate hook-to-bait length. The adjustable gap is between the lowest shot and the baited hook.

A longer gap gives the bait more freedom to drift and sink slowly. Too long a gap can let the bait wander, lift in current or move before the float clearly registers a bite. A shorter gap brings the weight closer, making the bait more controlled but less free-moving. Neither arrangement disconnects the line from the rod.

**Slack** means loose or bowed line, not a loose knot. It can appear without retying: current, wind, a drifting float or a fish swimming towards you can change the distance between the ends. A pull must first take up loose line before it reaches the rod clearly.

![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/float-line-slack.svg|600]]

Watch the float for bites. Gently reel in excess line between the rod tip and float, stopping before you drag it or pull the bait out of its natural drift. Below the float, the weights help the bait sink and the line hang down; current can still bend it. You do not need to stretch the whole rig tight while waiting for a bite.

topics.title: Swivels, snaps & leaders
topics.left: A barrel swivel joins line sections and helps reduce twist. A snap is a clip for quick tackle changes; check it closes properly and matches the tackle strength.
topics.right: The section nearest the hook. Choose strength for fish and structure; inspect for abrasion. A swivel can stop a sliding sinker before it reaches the leader.
topics.caption: Main line connects to one end of the swivel; the leader connects to the other.

note_sections.title: Why line gets curly or tangled
note_sections.text:
A line can hang loose without being damaged. Persistent coils or loops twisting around themselves point to different problems. These drawings show the difference; they are not photographs.

| Problem | Small visual | What it looks like | Common causes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Line memory** | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/line-memory.svg\|140]] | One strand keeps spring-like coils even when it is taken off the reel. | Nylon or fluorocarbon takes the curved shape of its spool; stiffness and long storage can make it more noticeable. |
| **Line twist** | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/line-twist.svg\|140]] | A loose section spins, doubles back or wraps around itself. | A rotating bait or lure, winding against slipping drag, or twist introduced while spooling. |
| **Ordinary slack / loose winding** | ![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/loose-line.svg\|140]] | The line hangs in a bow; loose loops may sit on the reel. | More line is out than the distance requires, or it was retrieved with too little tension. An overfilled spool can shed loops. |

Memory and twist can occur together. A sketch or description alone cannot confirm which is affecting a particular reel.

note_sections.title: Why cutting off a section can help
note_sections.text:
Removing an outer section may remove concentrated twist, kinks or abrasion. It also reduces the amount on the spool, which can improve an overfilled reel. The line underneath was already there; it is not necessarily newer or free of memory.

Cutting is not the first fix for ordinary slack. Take up loose line first. Replace visibly damaged or repeatedly troublesome line; do not keep cutting until the reel is too empty to cast properly.

note_sections.title: Prevent memory and twist on a spinning reel
note_sections.text:
1. **Match line to the reel.** Thick, stiff line is harder to manage on a small spinning reel. Use the line size and fill guidance for your reel; a supple line suited to it is easier to cast.
2. **Spool evenly under light tension.** Follow the reel and line maker’s loading method. Check for twist as you go and do not fill above the reel’s fill mark. A tackle shop can load replacement line.
3. **Close the bail by hand after casting.** The bail is the curved metal arm around the spool. Check that the line is seated on its roller and take up excess slack before retrieving.
4. **Fix loose loops before the next cast.** Stop, open the bail and carefully pull out line until the trapped loop is clear, then wind it back evenly with gentle tension. Do not cast the loop or yank a tightened knot through the guides.
5. **Check for unwanted spinning.** Straighten a bait or lure that rotates when it should not. A suitable swivel can reduce rotation passed to the line, but it does not remove line memory or fix loose winding.
6. **Let the drag work.** If the fish is pulling line off a spinning reel, avoid winding continuously against the slipping drag. Recover line when the fish eases.
7. **Check the used section.** Look and feel for roughness, flattened spots or kinks after a snag. Remove damaged line and retie; replace the line if the problem persists.

With a float rig, maintain contact without dragging the float: gently recover extra line between rod and float, while letting the bait drift. See [[Hobbies/Fishing/Rigs/Float rig#Bait distance, slack and bite contact|slack and bite contact]].

topics.title: Running sinker rig
topics.left: Slide a ball sinker onto main line, then tie a swivel. Tie leader to its other end and a single hook to the leader. A bead can protect the knot.
topics.right: Bottom bait fishing for bream, flathead or catfish. Start with a light sinker and adjust to flow. Keep bait near the feeding zone and the hook point clear.
topics.caption: Main line > sliding sinker > swivel > leader > hook. The weight slides; the swivel stops it.

topics.title: Float rig
topics.left: Fix a stem float on the line; add split shot below it and tie the hook. Adjust shot until the float stands with its tip visible.
topics.right: Set the hook depth near the weed or structure fish feed around. Drift bait naturally; adjust depth if it drags or stays above the feeding zone.
topics.caption: Float above, split shot below, hook at feeding depth. Change the float position to set depth.

note_sections.title: What the pieces do
note_sections.text:
A rig is the arrangement of tackle on your line. In a float rig, the float stays at the surface, small weights sink the bait, and the hook holds it below the water.

From rod towards bait: **line → float → split-shot weights → hook with bait**. This is the order along the line, not a drawing to scale.

note_sections.title: Set up a fixed float
note_sections.text:
1. Attach the float using its line guide and retaining sleeve; follow the instructions for that model.
2. Tie the hook to the end of the line and pinch split shot onto the line below the float. Split shot are small weights with a slit. Keep them above the hook so the bait can move.
3. Test it in the water. Add small amounts of weight until the float stands upright with its tip visible. If it sinks without a bite, remove weight.
4. Put the bait on the hook, leaving the point exposed.

note_sections.title: Choose the depth and watch for a bite
note_sections.text:
The distance from float to hook sets the approximate bait depth. For example, a hook 1 metre below the float hangs roughly 1 metre underwater when the line is vertical. Current can lift it or pull the line sideways.

Move the fixed float farther from the hook to fish deeper, or closer to fish shallower. Start near the depth of the weed-covered rocks where luderick feed, keeping the hook clear of snags.

Let the bait travel with the current; this is a drift. Take up loose line without dragging the float. For a luderick sneck hook, gently raise the rod when the float goes under from a bite. A snag or wave can also pull it down. Circle hooks need a different response: wind steadily rather than striking.

note_sections.title: Where to put split shot
note_sections.text:
Split shot is pinched onto the fishing line, not tied on. Put the line into the slit and close it gently so the weight stays in place. Some removable models have tabs for opening them again. If a shot slides freely, it is not gripping properly; reposition or replace it rather than crushing the line.

Place it **below the float and above the hook**. For a luderick rig, keep the lowest shot about **20 cm or more above the hook** as a starting arrangement, then adjust for the bait, float and current. This is not a fixed distance for every rig.

![[Hobbies/Fishing/Assets/split-shot-placement.svg|600]]

topics.title: Paternoster rig
topics.left: Tie main line to a swivel and attach a leader below it. Make one short hook dropper above a sinker tied to the bottom end.
topics.right: Bottom fishing in deeper water. The sinker reaches the bed while the hook sits above it. Keep the dropper short enough to limit tangles.
topics.caption: The weight is fixed at the bottom; the hook branches off above it.

topics.title: Bait & landing
topics.left: Thread bait neatly and leave the point and gape clear. Check it after small bites. Wet and tighten knots, then pull-test before casting.
topics.right: Use a wet net, support the body, and keep time out of water short. If deeply hooked, cut line near the mouth. Watch spines and keep fingers away from gills.
topics.caption: Leave the hook point clear. Use a wet net and support the fish when landing it.

topics.title: Tides & reading the water
topics.left: The curve shows water height over time. Rising is toward high tide; falling is toward low tide. Spring tides have a larger range; neap tides have a smaller range.
topics.right: Look for water moving past edges, bringing food. High/low tide does not always mean slack current: local flow can lag. Use local tide times and observe conditions. A tide curve is not a swell forecast.
topics.caption: High and low are water levels; rising and falling are the changes between them.
